name: Apollo 16 rover
intro: This rover carried John Young and Charlie Duke about 27 km across the Descartes highlands in April 1972. Its last job was to film Orion’s liftoff with its TV camera. It is still parked where they left it.
status: Parked forever where it filmed liftoff

hotspots.title: The Grand Prix
hotspots.text: On the first moonwalk, Young drove fast, braked and swerved while Duke filmed, so engineers could see how the rover handled. It bounced so hard that its wheels left the ground.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 16 video library

hotspots.title: Steering stick
hotspots.text: There is no steering wheel: the driver steered, sped up and braked with this one T-shaped stick. Both the front and rear wheels could steer.

source.label: NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

hotspots.title: The batteries
hotspots.text: Two 36-volt batteries powered the rover, and they could not be recharged. Once they ran down, the rover was finished for good.

source.label: NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

hotspots.title: The TV camera
hotspots.text: Controllers in Houston steered this camera by remote. On 24 April 1972 it followed Orion’s top half as it blasted off.

hotspots.title: The last parking spot
hotspots.text: Young drove the rover to this final spot at the end of the third moonwalk, a short distance east of Orion, so its camera could see the liftoff.

photo.caption: John Young drives to the final parking place on 23 April 1972.

funFact: The wheels have no air inside: their tyres are woven from steel wire, with titanium treads.
whyLeft: It was always a one-trip car: its batteries could not be recharged, and the astronauts parked it where its camera could film their liftoff.
repurpose: With new batteries and solar panels it might drive again, but that would break the rules protecting Apollo sites. Close-up photos of its wire wheels would help design tyres for new Moon rovers.
